newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem leading Serb in Bosnia's presidential race.
newsitem.headline: Moslem leading Serb in Bosnia's presidential race.

text.p: Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem, took a big lead over the top Serb candidate for the senior spot in a new collective presidency after post-war elections, early returns showed on Monday.

Izetbegovic had 170,107 votes to 121,391 for Momcilo Krajisnik, speaker of parliament in the separatist Serb entity of Bosnia, with 38 of 109 municipalities reporting, said the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.

The leader of Bosnia's main Moslem nationalist party also had an 82 percent to 15 percent lead over his opposition rival for the Moslem seat on the three-seat presidency, former prime minister Haris Silajdzic.
Krajisnik, a hard-line nationalist, was also far ahead of his Serb opposition rival for the presidency, with 78 percent of the vote compared to 19 percent for moderate Mladen Ivanic.
But while eastern Bosnia is a bastion of Krajisnik's Serb Democratic Party (SDS), around 70 percent of Bosnian Serbs live in the north where an opposition coalition is most popular.
Krajisnik's lead looked less assured in the northern town of Banja Luka, where he had 60 percent against 30 percent for Ivanic, with 70 percent of the votes counted.
In the race for the Croat seat on the presidency, nationalist Kresimir Zubak had 84 percent to 15 percent for centrist competitor Ivo Komsic.

Izetbegovic's party had feared Silajdzic might split the Moslem vote, allowing a Serb to emerge as head of the presidency. The senior member would act as Bosnia's head of state in foreign relations but the presidency will govern by consensus.
Final results for the presidency will be released on Tuesday.
A team of international observers found no major irregularities, its director said in a preliminary report on Monday.

The generally upbeat post-mortem by chief observer Ed van Thijn, Coordinator for International Monitoring, made it likely the OSCE would certify the election outcome despite fraud allegations by parties and voters.

But van Thijn's report was larded with caveats. He said the OSCE should demand the dominant Bosnian Serb separatist party amend its charter to endorse a reunified Bosnia as a condition for validating the elections.

Van Thijn also urged the OSCE not to stage municipal elections later this year as planned unless a problem with rigged voter lists was rectified and freer movement was established across Bosnia's internal ethnic boundaries.
Van Thijn, the Coordinator for International Monitoring in Saturday's elections, said almost 1,000 observers covered 65 percent of 4,440 polling stations in 87 of 109 districts.
He stressed at a news briefing that his report was preliminary and should be "treated with caution".

"(But), in our opinion, the elections were technically well prepared and carried out successfully under difficult circumstances," he said, alluding to the virulent hostility enduring between Serb, Moslem and Croat communities.

Monitors reported three notable problems with the conduct of the September 14 elections: Names missing or improperly registered at 56 percent of polling stations, polling stations overwhelmed by large crowds of voters, and refugees unable to safely reach balloting centres in Serb-controlled areas from which they were evicted in war except along 19 routes guarded by NATO peacekeepers.
Only 14,700 of a possible 150,000 refugees actually crossed communal lines to vote, many for fear of being assaulted. Van Thijn called this figure "very, very disappointing and unacceptable".
